newsitem.title: GREECE: Greek conservatives take thin lead ahead of vote.
newsitem.headline: Greek conservatives take thin lead ahead of vote.

text.p: Greece's main opposition conservatives hold a narrow lead over the ruling socialists just two weeks before national elections, the first major opinion poll of the campaign showed on Sunday.
Miltiades Evert's conservatives had 31 percent and Prime Minister Costas Simitis' socialists 30.6 percent in the nationwide opinion poll by the private MRB group.

Commentators presenting the poll on Mega television channel said that if confirmed on election day, the conservatives would probably be able to form a single-party government. The election law strongly favours the first party past the post.

Simitis's socialists were being badly hurt by three left-wing parties which were siphoning off votes. The DIKKI party, set up by former socialist finance minister Dimitris Tsovolas, took six percent in the opinion poll.

The Coalition of the Left, which failed to win a seat in the 300-seat parliament in November 1993, had 4.2 percent and the Communist Party had 4.9 percent. A party must win three percent of the national vote to take a seat in parliament.
Tsovolas, who once had his political rights suspended by a special criminal court, was confirmed as one of Greece's most popular politicians with 49.4 percent in the popularity section.

Underlining that Simitis's problems were more from the left than the right, Coalition of the Left leader Nikos Konstandopoulos headed the personal popularity sweepstakes with 51.9 percent. Simitis had 48.9 percent and Evert 36.4 percent.
Evert's party was boosted by the poor showing of the nationalist Political Spring party, which broke away from the conservatives several years ago and won 10 seats in parliament in the 1993 election.
Political Spring, headed by former conservative foreign minister Antonis Samaras, scored just three percent in the poll, the minimum for getting a deputy into parliament.

The poll showed voters to be largely disinterested in the election, which Simitis called a year early to cement his grip on power. More than 50 percent said they had little or no interest in the September 22 vote.
Simitis was elected premier by the socialist parliamentary group in January when the late socialist party founder Andreas Papandreou resigned in poor health.
He has a flat professorial style and has taken a high-brow stand, arguing that Greece must fight to secure its place as a fully accepted member of the European Union.

Evert, with a more animated, populist style, has stuck to bread and butter issues, pledging more money for farmers and pensioners and telling each district what specific measures he would take to help them.
Earlier in the day, Simitis hammered home his message that Greece could no longer afford to dole out favours to special interest groups and must focus on meeting EU economic targets.
"Things will not change with theatrics," Simitis told a news conference. "We are not here to impress voters...but to lay out our plans for a stronger Greece with an equal place in the EU."
He pledged an all-out attack on Greece's booming black economy, estimated at one third of the country's GDP and to restructure the public sector where hiring would be limited.

Evert has had stiff opposition from within his conservative party since taking over as leader in 1993 but the poll is likely to lift conservative hopes of returning to power in the closing weeks of the campaign.
